state.task: Select a candidate rendering representation for twenty hand-written .can-to-JavaScript target examples. This task designs the desired result and leaves compilation and dependency bodies unimplemented. The user considers the existing imported rendering functions excessively abstract, asks for a more direct declaration-to-output translation and rejects large HTML strings for poor readability. Their suggestion of Preact is exploratory, not approval. Business authority and access rules stay on the server. The user has now asked whether browser business state or logic could be beneficial; that is being evaluated independently rather than prohibited or accepted by this representation choice. This exercise provisionally retains server rendering with HTMX and does not implement a client-state architecture.
state.source: CanLang's adoption-oriented syntax lets AI generate concise CRUD/business SaaS for workerd. The single bounded presentation catalog rests on daisyUI and HTMX. Authored views use page/card/list/table/board/text/details/drawer/edit/actions/form/history/metrics/tabs/calendar/copy. Output must retain the access check on each page, current row/field grants, parent and record identity, operation arguments, ordering/search/filter/default behavior and English/Dutch inline translations. Owning operation declarations remain the unique schema source for both forms and MCP. Shell and component/widget bodies, protected reads, authorization, exact display, locale selection and full-page/partial-response handling are future shared imports rather than implementations included here. Do not invent additional app behavior or authoring syntax.
state.current: The existing proposals use functions with positional parameters: card(view,caption,()=>[...]), board(view,model,options,(row,view)=>[...]) and form(view,operation,{arguments:...}). They honestly declare their imports unimplemented, yet fail the user's desire to see a clear translation shape. The agreed artifact location/format is a valid JavaScript .mjs next to its .can. Choosing JSX-only text would force a transform or altered output file; h() and tagged templates already fit JavaScript. Short authored DSL does not oblige its expanded output to have the same token count.
state.evidence: Preact defines h(type,props,...children)/createElement for creating virtual nodes in its API guide (https://preactjs.com/guide/v11/api-reference/). An independent package, preact-render-to-string, emits HTML synchronously or through async/Web Streams APIs (https://preactjs.com/guide/v11/server-side-rendering/). Serializing on the server can feed HTML to HTMX without calling browser render/hydrate. The existing HTM package supplies tagged templates bound to h() and constructs trees rather than manually joined HTML (https://github.com/developit/htm). It nevertheless carries parsing/caching code and HTML-shaped literal source; long uses could reproduce the human's string-readability objection. Documentation establishes these interfaces, not proven workerd compatibility or bundle size for pinned package versions. Those require a subsequent real build exercise.
state.htmx: The official HTMX guide describes attribute-driven HTTP exchanges that usually return HTML, with hx-post/hx-target/hx-swap specifying submission and replacement (https://htmx.org/docs/). Selection of authorized fragments versus complete documents is server work; an HX-Request header conveys rendering preference and cannot authorize anything. Standard/shared behavior still protects focus and unsaved input and manages open controls and validation feedback. HTMX removes no such obligations and requires no separate application-data store in the browser. Either element trees or expanded HTML leave the relevant guarantees to actual runtime code. Keep all claims about missing dependencies provisional.
state.alternatives: Each candidate preserves server business bodies and owning metadata, numeric exactness, permissions, translated text, HTMX behavior and omitted library code. Component expansion and expression syntax are independent choices. Recognizable catalog components with named properties and nested nodes correspond closely to the DSL while leaving their markup unseen. Predominantly native HTML nodes make daisyUI layout and HTMX attributes visible while still importing necessary canonical forms/history/collection controls; this expands output and repeats uniform layout decisions. Collection callbacks belong in renderRow props to preserve row/view scope rather than ordinary vnode children. Plain h() expressions reuse Preact and the server serializer without a markup parser, with a verbosity cost. Short HTM trees use markup-like tagged syntax without JSX compilation, with additional parsing/cache machinery and literal source. Either expression form can build either component shape. Select neither dimension when evidence or human intent remains inadequate. These are revisable target examples, not immutable language promises. No renderer, framework, client application or authored manifest will be implemented.
state.client_evidence: Separate local visual interaction (focus, panels, selection and pending feedback), not-yet-persisted business drafts, readable-record caches, optimistic provisional mutations and execution of business rules in the browser. The app requirements already call for input preservation and pending/error handling. Sales stage/outcome changes, submitted document revisions/reviewer assignments, café availability, inventory balances and absence coverage all require current server authority. Feedback’s prescribed UI confirms votes without an unconfirmed counter increase. Field constraints can drive fast browser schema checks, but complete operation guards/invariants must remain canonical server checks for both MCP and web callers. Pure advisory evaluation or record caching may lower latency, save reads and synchronize views; it also needs exact numbers/time, permission-safe data, invalidation, concurrent-state reconciliation and honest pending/failure feedback. No observed device/latency/cache data or authored offline/cross-page transaction need proves a general store worthwhile. These missing measurements do not establish that such an approach has no value.
state.client_sources: The HTML specification defines browser constraint-validation facilities (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#the-constraint-validation-api). HTMX’s APIs cover request synchronization, pending-control disabling and preservation, while documenting focus/caret limitations on text inputs (https://htmx.org/attributes/hx-sync/, https://htmx.org/attributes/hx-disabled-elt/, https://htmx.org/attributes/hx-preserve/). TanStack provides separate UI-pending and cache-mutation approaches with cancel/snapshot/rollback/refetch duties (https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/optimistic-updates); React specifies transient optimism and failed-action recovery (https://react.dev/reference/react/useOptimistic). Such documentation demonstrates possibilities and coordination cost, not measured adoption impact or an approved dependency. One semantic CanLang compiler can target server JavaScript and any justified client projections/assets from one checked source; extra files do not necessitate multiple DSL compilers. More client semantics still bring checking, protocol and runtime complexity. Reused bundlers/library compilation are distinct from language analysis. The request authorizes evaluation, not construction, of client business state or rules.
state.async_scope: Normal Preact children cannot implicitly evaluate asynchronous record callbacks, await can_work or resolve arbitrary Promise nodes. The current pages require those guards and protected collection bindings. Library contracts must state how authorized bounded data and renderRow scope are prepared, or how a documented supported async-rendering API is used. This unimplemented responsibility is common across the tree alternatives and supplies no evidence for client caching.

granularity.instructions: Select component granularity on its own merits: recognizable source structure, visible HTML, expanded detail and shared canonical duties. Component names and explicit elements both leave correctness unproven. This question must neither prejudge the separate browser-state inquiry nor trigger an implementation of it.

criteria.catalog: Construct a nested tree of imported canonical catalog components with named props. It offers direct source-declaration recognition and uniform shared behavior, at the price of omitted component HTML and possible continued abstraction for the human.
criteria.native: Render app layout chiefly as HTML-tag nodes with daisyUI CSS and visible HTMX behavior, importing the necessary specialized canonical forms/controls. It offers inspectable markup, at the price of more output, repeated uniform layout and looser one-primitive correspondence.
criteria.unresolved: Leave component granularity undecided when the user’s desired relationship to source versus markup cannot be confidently inferred. Show an actual small app fragment in competing forms before bulk changes.

notation.instructions: For valid direct JavaScript trees, decide notation separately from how far components expand. Assess existing-library dependencies, code visibility and readability. Recognize that tagged HTM constructs vnodes rather than concatenated HTML without assuming its literals satisfy this user’s preference.

criteria.h: Use Preact’s ordinary h(type,props,...children) calls with the existing HTML serializer on the server. It requires neither a markup parser nor JSX stage and shows JavaScript structure, though deeply nested calls may be noisy.
criteria.htm: Use small nested HTM tagged trees bound to Preact and serialized server-side. It supplies HTML-style reading in plain JavaScript, while adding parser/cache code and markup literals that may remain hard for the user to read.
criteria.unresolved: Keep the h()/HTM notation decision open when its readability implications are not established; prepare a short concrete comparison.

client_scope.instructions: For these existing business apps, what initial browser responsibilities are justified? Balance responsive feedback, fewer reads and coordinated screens with adoption, compact authored source, one owning operation and output/runtime/compiler burden. Every alternative retains server authority and MCP/web consistency. Treat the former aversion to stores as a preference under renewed evaluation.

criteria.server_baseline: Retain HTMX server rendering, standard draft/visual/pending/error behavior and native field validation derived from schemas, without an initial general record cache or client business-rule projection. This minimizes coordination duties while retaining round trips for cross-field and stored-data feedback.
criteria.derived_preview: Generate advisory browser previews from pure, permission-safe canonical declarations for cross-field checks or precise derived totals, alongside local drafts/interaction. Retain server validation and omit a broad cache. This can improve instant feedback but adds eligibility analysis, exact adapters and generated browser code.
criteria.hydrated_store: Adopt a general nonauthoritative cache of business records with optimistic changes and eligible projected rules, using the same authoritative server operations. This can speed and coordinate views while adding client delivery, sync, rollback and permission/freshness invalidation.
criteria.unresolved: Reserve judgment on client scope pending specific UX/latency evidence and implementation-cost comparisons for previews and a wider browser record store.
